blocks.h: Why a dict of pair sums?
p: The triple loop is O(n³). Counting pairs by remainder reduces the third element's lookup to O(1), so the total is O(n²).

2964.takeaway: For each k, count earlier pairs whose sum has remainder (−nums[k]) mod d, stored in a dict of remainders.

p: `source = "abcd"`, `target = "acbe"` with rules a→b 2, b→c 5, c→b 5, c→e 1, e→b 2, d→e 20:
bullets: Total: 28. The direct rule c→b costs 5, but the chain c→e→b costs 1 + 2 = 3, which Floyd–Warshall finds; d→e costs 20, and a→a costs 0.

p: Conversions can chain (a→b then b→c), so the cost to convert one letter to another is the shortest path in the conversion graph. With only 26 letters Floyd–Warshall costs 26³ operations and then every position is an O(1) lookup.

2976.takeaway: Floyd–Warshall on 26 letters, then sum the cheapest conversion for each position.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: any(x % m for x in nums)
If some element is not a multiple of m, then x % m is a smaller positive number that can be produced and then eats everything else: the answer is 1
Otherwise only copies of m survive; each operation on two copies of m removes both and adds a 0 (m % m), and pairs of m's eventually leave ceil(count / 2) elements

p: `[5,5,5,10,5]`: the minimum is 5 and every element is a multiple of 5.

The operation picks two positive elements and replaces them with the remainder of one modulo the other. If some element x is not a multiple of the minimum m, then x % m is a positive value smaller than m; once such a smaller element exists, it can reduce every other element, and the array can be shrunk to a single element. If every element is a multiple of m, every remainder is 0 or comes from two equal copies of m, so only the copies of m pair off, leaving ceil(count / 2). I checked this formula against a brute-force search over small arrays and it matched every time.

3012.takeaway: If any number is not a multiple of the minimum the answer is 1, otherwise ceil(count of minimum / 2).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Walking along the street between houses i and j
Go from i to house x, take the shortcut road x–y (1 step), then walk from y to j
The shortcut used in the other direction
Counts the ordered pairs (i, j) and (j, i) at distance d

p: `n = 5`, shortcut between houses 2 and 4. Pairs where the shortcut gives a shorter path than the street:
The shortest route is either along the street only, or uses the shortcut once, entering at x or at y. Using the shortcut twice never helps. So the answer is the minimum of these three.

3015.takeaway: For each pair take min(direct, via x→y, via y→x) and count it twice (ordered pairs).

blocks.h: Why check only the largest side?
p: The triangle inequality must hold for all three pairs. If the sum of the two smaller sides exceeds the largest, then the other two inequalities (a + c > b, b + c > a) hold automatically, since c ≥ b and c ≥ a.

3024.takeaway: Sort the sides, check a+b > c, and name the type from the number of distinct lengths.

What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Trie edge labelled with the pair (i-th letter from the front, i-th letter from the back); creates the child if missing
Walking two ends of a string at once

Every earlier word that ends at a node on this path is both a prefix and a suffix of w
Registers the current word after counting

p: `["a","aba","ababa","aa"]` (each word's pairs are (front letter, back letter)):

head: word
earlier words that are a prefix and suffix
total

p: Let u have k letters and be an earlier word. Its path is the pairs (u[i], u[k−1−i]) for i < k. The first k pairs of w are (w[i], w[n−1−i]). Matching them means u[i] == w[i] (u is a prefix of w) and u[k−1−i] == w[n−1−i] (u is the last k letters of w, read backwards, i.e. a suffix). So one walk along w's path meets every earlier word that is both a prefix and a suffix of w.

3045.takeaway: Trie over pairs (front letter, back letter); end counters give the number of earlier words that are both prefix and suffix.

The statement defines exactly one rule per element, so following it directly is both simple and O(n). Version II adds a counting rule that needs a data structure (Fenwick tree).

head: Code
What it does

Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree): point update and prefix count in O(log m)
greaterCount(arr1, x): elements of arr1 strictly greater than x = size minus how many are ≤ x
If counts tie, the shorter array gets x; if lengths also tie, arr1

blocks.h: Why a Fenwick tree per array?
p: For each new element we need 'how many existing elements are greater' in both arrays. Re-counting is O(n); a Fenwick tree answers prefix counts and absorbs inserts in O(log n), so the whole process is O(n log n).

3072.takeaway: Two Fenwick trees over compressed ranks give 'count greater than x' in each array; apply the tie rules.

What it does

Distances from the start and from the end (graph is undirected, so Dijkstra from the end gives distances to the end)
Two sweeps instead of one per edge
Edge (u, v) lies on a shortest path if going start → u, across the edge, then v → end costs exactly the shortest distance (check both directions)

p: 6 nodes, 8 roads. Distances from node 0: `[0, 4, 1, 2, 7, 5]`, to node 5: `[5, 1, 4, 3, 2, 0]`; shortest total = 5:
bullets: Result: `[True, True, True, False, True, True, True, False]`.

p: Testing each edge by recomputing a shortest path would be one Dijkstra per edge. Two runs give every needed distance: an edge belongs to some shortest path iff it can be inserted between a shortest prefix and a shortest suffix without exceeding the optimum.

3123.takeaway: Dijkstra from both ends; an edge is on a shortest path iff d_start[u] + w + d_end[v] equals the shortest distance.

p: `nums = [1,2,1,1,3]`, `k = 2`: the table best_at[j] (longest subsequence with at most j changes) after all numbers:

Appending the same value as the last element costs nothing (`end[x][j]`), while appending a different value costs one change and can build on the best subsequence overall (`best_at[j−1]`). Keeping both makes each step O(k).

blocks.h: Why take all copies of a value?
p: If you cast one spell of damage v, the values v − 2 .. v + 2 (other than v itself) are blocked, and other spells of damage v are not. So taking all copies is free and strictly better than taking some.

3186.takeaway: Group by damage value; take-or-skip DP where taking v requires the best total of values ≤ v − 3 (found by bisect).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Number of suffix flips done so far (each flip inverts every element from the chosen index to the end)
Counting operations instead of performing them
Parity of flips: an odd count means the current element is inverted
XOR (exclusive or) gives the element's current value
A current 0 must be fixed now by flipping from here to the end

p: Scanning left to right, the only operation that changes the current element without disturbing the already-fixed prefix is a flip starting here. So a 0 must be flipped immediately, and counting the parity avoids actually flipping the suffix (which would be O(n²)).

3192.takeaway: Left-to-right greedy with a flip counter's parity: a current 0 forces a suffix flip.
